source.title: Open Problems on Information and Feedback Controlled Systems

accepted.question_text: For a feedback-controlled dynamical system in which a controller uses information about the system state to choose actions, how much can the system's performance be increased for a given amount of information? Equivalently, what quantitative bounds relate the amount of system-state information used by the controller to the attainable performance increase, including measures such as power output or efficiency?

evidence.quote: The questions we have selected mainly concern the establishment of bounds to the performance and the establishment of the thermodynamics of feedback controlled systems.
the first natural main question is how much the performance can be increased with a certain amount of information

accepted.question_text: How can the thermodynamics of feedback-controlled systems be formulated so that the thermodynamic effects of information transfer between the system and the controller are explicitly accounted for? The formulation should support thermodynamic quantities and limits such as maximum efficiency and bounds on work that can be extracted from the feedback-controlled system.

evidence.quote: The second main question is the establishment of the thermodynamics of feedback controlled systems accounting for thermodynamic effects of the information transfer.
the computation of the maximum efficiency involves a bound in the work that can be extracted from the feedback controlled system

accepted.question_text: For correlated repeated actuation of a feedback controller, what is the precise relationship between entropy-reduction results derived from the viewpoint of the feedback-controlled system and Zurek's algorithmic-complexity approach, which treats the system plus controller together? In particular, how does the minimum energetic cost for erasing the controller's stored measurement record correspond to thermodynamic constraints on the maximum entropy reduction of the controlled system?

evidence.quote: One particular open question involves the precise relations between these recent results and the algorithmic complexity approach adopted by Zurek
This study has allowed Zurek to establish the minimum energetic cost for erasing a memory that has stored the measurements the controller has processed
This minimum energetic cost also sets thermodynamic constraints that lead to a maximum entropy reduction for the system.

accepted.question_text: Can entropy-reduction results for correlated repeated actuation by an external feedback controller be applied or extended to derive bounds for other performance measures of feedback-controlled systems, specifically including the maximum attainable flux and the maximum attainable power?

evidence.quote: the entropy reduction of a system due to the correlated repeated actuation of an external controller has been computed

Another open question is the application or the extension of the results found in [13] to find bounds for other performance measures of feedback controlled systems, for example, the maximum attainable flux or power.

accepted.question_text: When a feedback controller operates in the continuous-actuation limit, meaning that it repeatedly acts on the system with a period shorter than every characteristic time scale of the system dynamics, how can results for correlated repeated feedback actuation be extended to that limit despite the nontrivial relationship between differential entropy and discrete entropy?

evidence.quote: the controller repeatedly actuates on the system with a period shorter than any of the characteristic time scales of the system dynamics
the continuous time limit of the results found in [13] is not direct because of the nontrivial relationship between differential entropy and discrete entropy
Therefore, even the extension of the results in [13] to the continuous actuation limit remains still an open problem.

accepted.question_text: For feedback-controlled flashing ratchets, in which a controller uses information about the system state to rectify thermal fluctuations of Brownian particles by switching a periodic potential on and off, can the general entropy-reduction and thermodynamic results for feedback-controlled systems be applied to establish bounds on attainable entropy reduction and a thermodynamic description of these ratchets?

evidence.quote: a controller with information of the state of the system rectifies the thermal fluctuations of Brownian particles by switching on and off a periodic potential
The application of the results of [13] to feedback controlled flashing ratchets has not been done yet.
It will allow to establish bounds on the entropy reduction attainable for feedback flashing ratchet and to establish the thermodynamics of these systems

accepted.question_text: For feedback-controlled flashing ratchets, existing bounds relate flux improvement and power-output improvement to information used by the controller per actuation. How can those bounds be reformulated in terms of the total non-redundant information acquired per unit time, so that the ratchet bounds can be related to the entropy-reduction and thermodynamic framework for general feedback-controlled systems?

evidence.quote: relations between the information I (about the system) gathered by the controller per step and the performance have been recently obtained
These relation were stated in terms of the information per actuation.
total amount of information per unit time (i.e., only computing non-redundant information per unit time) is still an open question

accepted.question_text: In nanotechnology devices and biological systems where one part of the system improves the performance of another part through bidirectional interaction, what concrete limitations do information-theoretic and thermodynamic bounds for feedback-controlled systems impose on the operation and achievable performance of those devices and systems?
accepted.context_brief: Implications for nano and biological systems

evidence.quote: one is interested in increasing the performance of one part of the system through the bidirectional interaction of other part of the system
Finding these implications is still a very relevant open question.

trace.notes: Normalized the original zbMATH resolver URL. A local harvested zbMATH row identified the exact work as DOI 10.3390/e14040834 with arXiv link 1205.4434; the arXiv record confirmed the same title, journal reference, and related DOI. The MDPI DOI page was selected as the readable full-text HTML artifact.

Mapped the MDPI HTML article structure: title and bibliographic data, abstract, Section 1 introduction, Section 2 state of the art with definitions and prior bounds, Section 3 open problems with subsections on feedback-controlled systems, correlated repeated actuation, continuous actuation, feedback flashing ratchets, and nanotechnology/biological systems, followed by conclusions and references.

Extracted eight open-question candidates from the explicit open-problem region in Section 3: two broad main questions, two correlated-repeated-actuation questions, one continuous-actuation question, two feedback-flashing-ratchet questions, and one nanotechnology/biological-systems implications question.
Expanded the first main question into a standalone performance-bound problem and inlined the feedback-control setting and representative performance measures from the source.
Rewrote the second main question as a thermodynamic-framework problem and resolved the work/efficiency context from the same source sentence.
Resolved the Zurek cross-reference using adjacent source text that describes the algorithmic-complexity viewpoint, erasure cost, and entropy-reduction constraint.
Resolved the reference to the prior results as entropy-reduction results for correlated repeated actuation and preserved the source examples of flux and power.
Made the continuous-actuation limit self-contained by inlining the source definition and the differential-versus-discrete entropy obstacle.
Inlined the source description of feedback flashing ratchets and rewrote the application of prior results as a standalone thermodynamic-bounds problem.
Expanded the compressed per-actuation statement into a standalone question about total non-redundant information per unit time.
Rewrote the implications question to identify the relevant bidirectionally interacting nanotechnology and biological systems without relying on section context.

Kept eight distinct questions. The two broad main questions were retained separately from the more specific correlated-actuation, continuous-actuation, ratchet, and nano/bio implications questions because they ask at different levels of generality.

All accepted items are self-contained, carry explicit HTML line evidence, avoid unresolved source-pointing references in question_text, introduce no unsupported technical facts, and include solved-status metadata set to false because the source does not mark any item solved.
